findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches and executes arbitrary remote code as root during the image build with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no inspect step. Whatever that URL returns at build time is executed unconditionally; a compromised DNS/CDN/host or a mutable script silently changes the resulting image. This is a supply-chain/untrusted-code-execution surface newly introduced by this diff (the base Dockerfile has no such step).

findings.title: curl | sh masks download failure so build can succeed silently
findings.whyItBreaks: In `curl -sL ... | sh`, the RUN step's exit status is that of `sh`, not `curl`. When curl fails before producing output (DNS failure, connection reset, timeout), `sh` receives empty stdin and exits 0, so the image build reports success even though nothing was installed. The `-s` flag additionally suppresses curl's error output, so the failure leaves no diagnostic. The added step therefore cannot distinguish 'install failed' from 'install succeeded', and downstream `COPY app`/`CMD` build on a broken image.

findings.title: Do not curl|sh an unpinned remote script in the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches and executes whatever the remote endpoint serves at build time with root privileges, with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no integrity check. Anyone who can control DNS/TLS for the host or compromise the server gains arbitrary code execution inside the built image (and any build secret or layer output). Because the content is not pinned, builds are also non-reproducible and can silently change between runs. `-s` additionally suppresses transfer errors, and the pipe discards curl's exit status, so a failed fetch can still yield a 'successful' build via an empty script.

findings.title: Do not curl-pipe a remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes an unpinned, unverified remote script as root inside the image build. There is no checksum/signature pinning and no version pin: any compromise, DNS hijack, or content change at the URL yields arbitrary code execution in the built image (silent RCE via supply chain). It also makes the build non-reproducible and, because `curl` runs with `-s` and no `-f`, a failed/redirected request can still emit a body that is piped into `sh`.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing; missing key indistinguishable from empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load reports absence via ErrMissing (src/store.go:10), but LoadOrDefault discards that error with `v, _ := Load(...)` (src/store.go:16) and returns the zero value "". Because "" is also a legitimate value a key can hold (Load returns any present value verbatim at src/store.go:12), every caller of this exported helper is forced to conflate "key is missing" with "key is present and empty". A caller doing a load-modify-write (read, treat as current state, write back) cannot tell it needs to initialize vs. preserve an existing empty value, and will silently drop the failed-read signal instead of propagating it.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load signals a missing key by returning ErrMissing (src/store.go:10); LoadOrDefault at src/store.go:16 discards that error (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`) and returns the zero value "". Every eventual caller now receives the same "" for a missing key and for a key explicitly stored as the empty string, so it cannot tell absence from a legitimate value and will act on the fallback as real data (defaults, routing, persistence). Because this is an exported (public) API surface with no distinguishing return, the contract itself forces every caller into this conflation.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines deliver results; results lost
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, Run blocked on `results <- j*2` for every job, so returning from Run guaranteed every result had been enqueued/received by the consumer. After the change, Run spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no WaitGroup (or equivalent) to join them. Any caller that treats Run's return as completion — closes `results`, stops receiving, or counts `len(results)` — now observes zero/partial results and drops work. It also leaks goroutines: if the consumer stops receiving (e.g. an unbuffered or insufficiently buffered channel that is no longer drained after Run returns), every spawned goroutine blocks forever on the send. Result ordering is additionally no longer deterministic.

findings.title: Synchronize spawned senders before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run was synchronous: each `results <- j*2` completed inside the loop, so when Run returned every job had been delivered and the function implied a completion contract (fill the channel, then return). The edit moves the send into a fire-and-forget goroutine with no WaitGroup or channel-of-completion, so Run returns immediately while len(jobs) senders are still runnable. Two concrete consequences: (1) the idiomatic caller sequence `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` now panics with `send on closed channel` because goroutines reach `results <- j*2` after the caller closed the channel; (2) if the receiver stops draining, each blocked sender leaks forever. `ctx` is still ignored, so cancellation cannot unblock them either. The loop variable is correctly passed by value (`func(j int)` / `(j)`), so that is not the issue.

findings.title: Ensure Run waits for goroutines and preserves result ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Run was synchronous: the base body `results <- j * 2` blocked until every result was delivered, so when Run returned all sends had completed and results arrived in jobs order. The head body spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately. Consequences on any live path: (1) Run returns before any result is produced, so a caller that reads len(jobs) values from results, or treats Run's return as 'jobs done', now observes missing/early state; (2) a caller that closes results right after Run returns — safe before — now makes the still-pending goroutines panic with 'send on closed channel'; (3) results are emitted in nondeterministic order, breaking positional mapping results[i] <-> jobs[i]; (4) if the channel is full/unbuffered with no reader, or ctx is cancelled, the goroutines block forever and leak, and Run's unused ctx (@src/worker.go:5) gives them no way to stop.

findings.title: Fix authorization bypass from && to || in canDeleteRecord
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` (admin AND same tenant). The new disjunction `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` returns true in two previously-denied cases: (1) an admin of ANY tenant can delete a record in a DIFFERENT tenant (cross-tenant authorization bypass), and (2) any non-admin user in the record's tenant can delete it, ignoring `record.ownerId` (ownership check dropped). Delete-gating callers will now permit destructive actions that were previously rejected.

findings.title: Authorization bypass in canDeleteRecord (&& changed to ||)
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required BOTH session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. Changing && to || flips it from an AND-gate to an OR-gate, so two unauthorized cases now return true: (1) any admin deletes records in ANY tenant (session.isAdmin true regardless of tenant mismatch), and (2) any non-admin user deletes records in their own tenant (tenant match regardless of isAdmin false). The function is exported, so this loosened contract propagates to every caller; the exported signature carries no compensating check.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord AND→OR admits cross-tenant admins and any same-tenant user
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous contract required BOTH session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With `||`, the predicate returns true in two newly-wrong cases: (1) session.isAdmin=true but tenantId differs → an admin can delete records in ANY tenant (cross-tenant privilege escalation); (2) session.isAdmin=false but tenantId matches → any ordinary user in the same tenant can delete records (privilege escalation past the admin-only gate). This is an exported authorization predicate whose sole purpose is to gate the delete action, so the loosened result is an authorization bypass regardless of caller, not a benign widening.

findings.title: buildReport pairs branch commit with artifacts from unrelated "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code returned { builtFrom: commit, artifacts: build.artifactsAt(commit) }, so the reported commit and the artifacts came from the same ref. The new code returns artifacts from build.ref("verified") while builtFrom remains the branch commit, so the report's artifacts no longer correspond to the commit it claims they were built from. Whenever "verified" differs from the requested branch, the report is internally inconsistent: a consumer cannot tell which commit the artifact list describes, and any verification/audit use of buildReport silently attributes artifacts to the wrong commit. If the build has no "verified" ref, artifactsAt receives whatever build.ref returns (error or empty/undefined), changing behavior further.

The BuildReport contract pairs the reported commit with the artifacts that commit contains; before this change both came from the same `commit` variable. Now the report is internally inconsistent: `builtFrom` claims the branch commit while `artifacts` are the contents of an unrelated (hardcoded) ref, so any consumer that trusts builtFrom as the origin of the listed artifacts is misled, and the caller-supplied `branch` no longer influences artifact selection at all.

Now artifacts come from artifactsAt(ref("verified")) while builtFrom is still ref(branch). The branch argument no longer affects which artifacts are listed: calling buildReport(build, "main") and buildReport(build, "develop") returns different builtFrom values but identical artifacts (whatever the "verified" ref points at), so the report can misattribute a ref's artifacts to a commit that did not produce them.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against wrong revision than fromRevision

The diff adds `const latest = store.resolve("latest")` (line 15) and passes `latest` to readChangedPaths (line 18) while fromRevision remains `from` (line 17). The Store.readChangedPaths signature takes a `fromRevision`, so a caller replaying the returned paths onto `from` now receives a path set computed against `latest` (a different revision — e.g. empty or an unrelated diff), producing a wrong/incomplete replay. findings.title: Async reserve yields between check and write, allowing oversell race
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change reserve() was synchronous, so the read (line 15), emptiness check (line 16) and write-back (line 18) ran to completion without yielding, making the decrement atomic under JS's single-threaded model. The added `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) yields control after the check but before the in-memory write. Two concurrent reserve() calls for the same sku both read the same `remaining`, both pass `remaining <= 0`, both persist `remaining - 1` and both `return true`, so the method reports two successful reservations while stock drops by only one. With remaining=1 this oversells a single unit; with N concurrent callers all computing from the same stale value, it oversells by up to N-1.

findings.title: reserve() awaits between check and decrement, allowing concurrent oversell

Two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both observe the same `remaining`, both persist `remaining - 1` to the store, both set the same value, and both return true. Two reservations succeed while only one unit is consumed. In the base version the check-and-decrement was fully synchronous and therefore atomic in JS's single-threaded model; adding the await introduces the interleaving window, so this is a regression introduced by the diff (lost update / oversell).

findings.title: Await between read and write lets concurrent reserve oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: `reserve` reads remaining (line 15), then `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) yields the microtask queue, and only afterwards writes back to this.stock (line 18). Two concurrent `reserve('a')` calls on a stock of 1 both read remaining=1, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both persist save(sku, 0), and both return true — two units reserved from one (lost update / oversell). Before this PR the read-check-set was a single synchronous block, so calls could not interleave and the counter stayed consistent; the await point is what introduces the race.

Because `store.save` can reject, a caller that ignores the returned promise also gets an unhandled rejection instead of the previous plain `false`. With no in-repo callers to update, this ships as a silent contract break for external consumers.

Pre-change delays were a=0→1s, a=1→2s, a≥5→30s. Post-change they are a=0→1,000,000ms (1000s), a=1→2,000,000ms, capped at 30,000*1000 = 30,000,000ms (30,000s ≈ 8h20m). findings.title: Save discards f.Close() error, masking close-time write failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ended with `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), propagating the file-close error to the caller. The new code defers `f.Close()` (line 13) and returns only `w.Flush()` (line 20). bufio.Flush surfaces errors reported at Write() time, but an os.File created by os.Create can report write-back failures only at Close (delayed allocation/ENOSPC, NFS/SMB/FUSE writeback, quota errors). Those errors are now discarded, so Save returns nil even though the data was not durably written. Because Save is an exported function whose contract is to report write failures, a caller treating nil as 'persisted' will treat a failed save as success (data loss).

findings.title: Restore propagation of f.Close() error in Save

Now `defer f.Close()` (line 13) discards it, and `return w.Flush()` (line 20) only reports buffer-flush errors. For a file opened for writing, real write failures (deferred allocation, ENOSPC, NFS/EIO) are frequently surfaced only at Close, so Save now returns nil after a failed/partial write. Save is an exported symbol, so every caller is forced to conflate a failed persist with a successful one — silent data loss reported as success.

findings.title: Save discards f.Close error, hiding failed writes
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `Save` ended with `return f.Close()`, propagating any error the OS reports when flushing the file's buffers to durable storage (e.g. ENOSPC/EIO on delayed allocation or network filesystems). After the change, the final close runs in `defer f.Close()` and its error is discarded; the function's only returned error now comes from `w.Flush()` (line 20). `bufio.Writer.Flush` only pushes bytes into the OS, not to disk, so a genuine write failure surfaced at `Close` is swallowed and `Save` returns nil. `Save` is an exported function, so every caller is forced to treat `nil` as a successful, durable save while data may be unwritten — silent data-loss contract.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of each page (range end-1 off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds documents and returns half-open [start, end) (lib/pagination.py:17-21), but the rewritten loop iterates range(start, end - 1), excluding the last in-range index. Substituting real values: rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_index=0, page_size=2 -> start=0,end=2 -> range(0,1) returns [a] instead of [a,b]; page_index=2 -> start=4,end=min(6,5)=5 -> range(4,4) returns [] so row 'e' is lost entirely. The base implementation used range(start, end) (base lib/pagination.py:19) and returned the full page, so this is an introduced regression. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) and summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) both consume page_window, so every rendered page silently omits its last row and single-row pages render empty.

findings.title: Off-by-one drops last row of each page in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds (start = page_index*page_size, end = min(start+page_size, row_count) — see line 20 and docstring line 18), so the correct slice is an inclusive-of-end-1 loop `range(start, end)`. The new loop `range(start, end - 1)` excludes the final index of every window, so each full page renders page_size-1 rows instead of page_size, and the last page loses the final row of the dataset. Original code looped `range(start, end)` where end = min(start+size, len(rows)), so this is a regression introduced by this PR. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) consume this window, so the dropped rows are silently absent from all rendered output with no error.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation collected the half-open window with range(start, end). The refactor changed it to range(start, end - 1), which excludes index end-1, dropping the final row of every page. _window_bounds (line 18) still documents the range as half-open [start, end), so end-1 is a genuine off-by-one, not an inclusive-end adjustment. A page with a single row now returns an empty list (start=0, end=1 -> range(0,0)), so render_page returns an empty string and summarize silently omits that page's row entirely. Example: page_window([a,b,c,d], 0, 3) returns [a,b] instead of [a,b,c].

findings.title: Invert TtlCache expiry check; expired entries returned as valid
findings.whyItBreaks: `Date.now() - entry.storedAt` is the entry's age. Previously `age < ttlMs` returned a fresh entry's value and deleted+nulled expired ones. The change to `age > ttlMs` inverts the semantics: entries OLDER than the TTL are returned as if valid (stale reads), and FRESH entries are deleted on access and reported as a miss. Every consumer of this exported `TtlCache.get` now gets expired data or spurious misses — the class no longer behaves as a TTL cache.

findings.title: pruneDone splice-during-forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: `forEach` advances by array index while `splice` shifts later elements down, so a done job immediately following another done job is skipped. E.g. [done,done,notDone] -> index 0 spliced -> [done,notDone] -> index 1 is notDone -> returns [done,notDone], leaving a done job unpruned. The refactor also changes the contract: the original `jobs.filter(...)` returned a NEW array and left the argument untouched, whereas this version mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, so any caller still holding the original array sees it partially pruned.

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was inverted. Base: `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` returned the value only while it was still fresh, otherwise fell through to delete+return null. Now `> this.ttlMs` returns EXPIRED entries as if valid (TTL enforced nowhere, so stale values are served indefinitely) and deletes still-fresh entries, returning null for hits that should succeed. Every consumer gets the exact opposite of the documented TTL behavior on both branches.

findings.title: pruneDone skips done jobs after each splice
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering by splicing inside forEach shifts subsequent elements down while the iterator advances its index, so the element immediately following each removed job is never examined. With jobs [{done:true},{done:true}] the second done job is left in the result — the array is not actually pruned. The base `filter` handled every element.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates caller's input array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation was pure (returned a new filtered array). The rewrite splices the caller's array and returns the same reference, so any caller that still holds the original array now sees its done jobs silently destroyed — a side-effect data-loss regression that the function name/signature gives no hint of.

findings.title: TtlCache.get serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness predicate was flipped from `<` to `>`. With ttlMs=1000, an entry stored 100ms ago gives age=100; `100 > 1000` is false, so the fresh entry is deleted and null is returned. An entry stored 2000ms ago gives age=2000; `2000 > 1000` is true, so the stale value is returned. The cache now does the exact opposite of its contract: it reports expired data as valid and drops valid data.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs due to splice-in-forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element with splice while forEach advances its index skips the following element. For jobs=[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]: index 0 is done -> splice -> [{done:true},{done:false}]; iteration moves to index 1 = {done:false} (no removal); loop ends. The remaining done job is never pruned, so pruneDone returns [{done:true},{done:false}] instead of [{done:false}]. Any two adjacent done jobs are left in the result.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's input array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a filtered copy and left the caller's array untouched. The new implementation splices the argument directly and returns the same reference. A caller that still holds the original array (e.g. iterating it after calling pruneDone, or reusing it for audit/reporting) now sees elements silently removed.

findings.title: busiest() mutates the caller's array instead of a copy
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, busiest() sorted a defensive copy (`[...rows].sort(...)`); the change sorts `rows` in place. Any caller still holding the array it passed now has its element order silently reordered as a side effect, which corrupts unrelated logic that depends on insertion/input order (e.g. index-based access, 'first row' semantics, or re-aggregation). The exported function gives callers no indication of the mutation.

findings.title: averageAmount() returns NaN on empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` means an empty array evaluates `total / 0` as `0 / 0`, which is NaN, not 0. The previous contract returned a defined 0 for the empty case. NaN is type-`number` so it passes the declared return type unchecked, then silently poisons any downstream arithmetic/formatting (e.g. totals become NaN, displayed as 'NaN'), and NaN-derived comparisons are always false — the failure is silent rather than surfaced.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was the only protection against division by zero. With it gone, an empty `rows` array leaves `total = 0` (reduce initial value) and computes `0 / rows.length` = `0 / 0` = `NaN`. The function's declared return type is `number` and the base revision returned `0`, so downstream arithmetic/comparisons now silently propagate NaN instead of a usable zero.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The base body copied the input with `[...rows]` before sorting, so the caller's array was preserved. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)`, and `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place and returns the same reference. Any caller that passes its own array (or a slice it still uses) now has that array reordered as a side effect of calling a read-only-looking 'busiest' query — silent caller-data mutation.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard so averageAmount returns 0, not NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was deleted, so for an empty array `total` is 0 and `0 / rows.length` evaluates to `0 / 0 === NaN`. Callers that previously received the numeric default 0 now receive NaN, which silently poisons any downstream arithmetic, comparison, or serialization (NaN is not valid JSON and serializes to null). This is an observable behavior change on a changed line.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy so busiest does not mutate caller data
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and returns the same array reference, so this now mutates the caller's input array, reordering the caller's data as an undocumented side effect. Any caller that reuses its `rows` collection after calling `busiest` (rendering in insertion order, iterating, comparing to a saved snapshot, sharing with other logic) observes corrupted/reordered state. The prior copy prevented this; dropping it is a regression on a changed line.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending sort; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator orders numbers by their STRING form, then `.reverse()` gives descending string order, not descending numeric order. Substituting real values: players scores [100, 9, 2] -> sort() -> [100,2,9] -> reverse -> [9,2,100]. For n=3, cutoff = scores[min(3,3)-1] = scores[2] = 100, so filter(p.score >= 100) yields only the 100 player and slice(0,3) returns [100] — topPlayers returns 1 entry instead of all 3. Another case [30,4], n=2: reversed = [4,30], cutoff = scores[1] = 30, filter >= 30 returns only [30] instead of [30,4]. formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:19) consumes topPlayers, so displayed rankings omit legitimate players. This is a regression versus the base `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)`.

findings.title: rankScores sorts scores lexicographically, breaking top-N cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units, so numbers are ordered lexicographically, not numerically. The base version used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) (numeric descending). rankScores() now returns e.g. [3, 20] for inputs [3, 20], and the cutoff scores[Math.min(n, len)-1] is read off this wrong ranking, so topPlayers/formatBoard filter by an incorrect cutoff. Concrete: topPlayers([{name:'a',score:3},{name:'b',score:20}], 1) -> rankScores=[3,20], cutoff=scores[0]=3, filter score>=3 keeps both, slice(0,1) -> [{a,3}]; the correct answer is [{b,20}]. For [10,9,100] it returns only the 100 entry where the top-2 should be 100 and 10.

findings.title: Default sort ranks numeric scores lexicographically, breaking topPlayers
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed comparator sorted numerically descending (`(a,b)=>b-a`); the replacement calls `scores.sort()` with no comparator, so Array.prototype.sort converts each number to a string and orders by UTF-16 code units. For players [100,10,2] with n=2 the old code gave cutoff=scores[1]=10 and returned both a(100) and b(10); the new code sorts to [10,100,2], reverses to [2,100,10], sets cutoff=scores[1]=100, and filters p.score>=100, returning only one player and distorting formatBoard output. Any mixed-digit scores (e.g. 9 vs 10, 100 vs 2) are mis-ranked.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() gates the authentication decision in handle() (401 vs 200 at app/webhook.py:14-16). The previous code used hmac.compare_digest on the two hex digests, which runs in constant time. Replacing it with `==` compares bytes and short-circuits on the first mismatch, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the attacker-supplied signature match the expected MAC. An attacker can iteratively recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge webhook payloads, defeating the authenticity check this function exists to provide.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with Python's `==` string comparison. `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so its running time leaks how many leading hex characters of the attacker-supplied `given_signature` match the real digest. A remote caller hitting the webhook can measure per-request latency to iteratively recover the correct signature and bypass the 401 gate in `handle` (app/webhook.py:14), which is a security authentication bypass. This is a direct regression: the base revision used the constant-time primitive for exactly this reason.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously used hmac.compare_digest for a constant-time comparison of the computed and supplied HMAC-SHA256 signature; it now uses == , which short-circuits on the first differing byte. This is a classic timing side-channel (CWE-208) on a security-critical check: an attacker can iteratively guess the expected signature byte-by-byte by measuring response-time differences, and a forged signature makes handle() (app/webhook.py:14) treat an untrusted payload as authentic and run processor on it.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ran the INSERT and both UPDATEs inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled back all three. The new code (lines 22-24) commits the ledger INSERT when the `with` block exits, then calls `_apply_balances` (lines 8-16) AFTER the transaction has committed. If either UPDATE fails or the process dies between line 23 and line 24, the ledger records a completed transfer while one or both account balances are unchanged (or only debited, not credited) — money is recorded as moved but was not moved, and there is no rollback path. The `db.execute` return values are also unchecked, so a failed/ignored UPDATE still returns `{"ok": True}`.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs executed inside a single `with db.transaction():` scope, so any failure rolled back all three. Now only `_record_ledger` (line 23) is inside the transaction; `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs after the block exits, i.e. outside/after that transaction. If `_apply_balances` fails partway (e.g. the credit UPDATE errors, a constraint fires, process is killed), the ledger row and the sender debit are already committed while the recipient credit is not — permanently unbalanced books and lost funds, with no rollback path. The pre-change code rolled all three statements back together.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) executed inside `with db.transaction():`, so any failure rolled the whole transfer back. The refactor keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the context manager and calls `_apply_balances` after the `with` block exits (line 24). The context manager commits on exit, so the ledger row is persisted even if the subsequent balance updates fail; and if the second UPDATE in `_apply_balances` fails, the debit is applied while the credit is not (or vice versa). A money transfer can now leave a committed ledger entry with no/partial balance movement, i.e. an asymmetric or phantom transfer.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, making billing day timezone-dependent
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the day from UTC fields (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate), so a given instant mapped to exactly one billing day regardless of where it ran. The new line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process-local timezone. The same instant now yields different strings on different hosts: e.g. 2026-03-01T02:00:00Z is "2026-02-28" on a UTC-5 host but "2026-03-01" under UTC/TZ=Asia/Shanghai. This shifts the billing-day boundary, mis-assigns usage/charges across billing periods, and makes exported keys and sameBillingDay() comparisons non-deterministic across servers/timezones for identical inputs.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, making results server-timezone dependent
findings.whyItBreaks: The body replaced getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The result is now computed in the host's local timezone, so the identical instant (e.g. 2026-01-01T02:00:00Z) yields 2026-01-01 on a UTC server but 2025-12-31 on a server set to America/Los_Angeles. Billing is thus attributed to different calendar days depending on deployment TZ / DST, and sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the same shift, splitting or merging billing days for the same instant across machines. The prior implementation was deliberately UTC for a stable, global billing boundary.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, not UTC (TZ-dependent regression)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base computed the billing day from at.getUTCFullYear()/getUTCMonth()/getUTCDate(), so the same instant always produced the same 'YYYY-MM-DD' regardless of environment. Head uses at.getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate(), which read the process's local timezone. Two servers (or a single server whose TZ differs from UTC) now return different billing days for the same instant, and any timestamp within the local-UTC offset of midnight is classified one day off. Downstream consumers, including the unchanged sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) which compares billingDay output for equality, inherit the mis-classification.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, leaking one tenant's profile to another
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo is a single global Map keyed only by `account`. `account` is tenant-scoped (fetchProfile is called with both tenant and account, and Profile carries a tenant field), so two tenants with the same account id now share one cache entry. After tenant A populates memo['alice'], readProfile('tenantB', 'alice', ...) hits `if (cached) return cached` and returns tenant A's Profile without ever calling fetchProfile('tenantB','alice') — a cross-tenant data leak plus a wrong-tenant result.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile identity is the pair (tenant, account): the function takes both, passes both to fetchProfile(tenant, account), and Profile carries a tenant field. Keying the process-wide `memo` map by `account` alone makes tenant a non-factor, so readProfile('tenantA','alice') and readProfile('tenantB','alice') share one entry. Whichever call populates the map first serves its Profile object to every later tenant with a same-named account, returning a profile whose `tenant`/`displayName` belong to a different tenant (auth/isolation-relevant data disclosure, and stale or wrong profile for the second tenant). The previous key `${tenant}:${account}` was collision-free.

findings.title: Restore tenant in profile memo cache key to avoid cross-tenant collision
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` map is shared across all tenants, but the cache key is now only `account`. Transient `account` is tenant-scoped evidence: `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` (line 17) takes both, and `Profile` carries a distinct `tenant` field (line 2). When two tenants have an account with the same name, the second `readProfile` call returns the first tenant's cached `Profile` from `memo.get(key)` (line 15) without calling `fetchProfile`, yielding a wrong-tenant/leaked profile instead of that tenant's own profile. Previously the key `${tenant}:${account}` isolated tenants.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns ""
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change load() threw `missing: <key>` when store.get(key) was undefined, a distinct failure signal. The new try/catch maps that (and any other thrown error) to the legitimate in-band value "". The failure is no longer distinguishable from a real empty string, so every consumer is forced to treat a missing key as real data. TRIGGER D: this is an exported/public swallow site, so the broken contract ships regardless of in-repo callers. The one in-repo caller, loadAll (src/store.ts:12), now returns an array containing silent "" entries for any missing key instead of surfacing the error.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returning "" as a real value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: <key>` when the key was absent, letting callers distinguish a missing entry from an empty one. Now the catch-all returns "", and since the store type is Map<string,string>, "" is also a legitimate stored value. Any caller (including loadAll at src/store.ts:12) can no longer tell "key absent" from "key present with empty value", and failure silently flows onward as data. load() is exported, so every eventual external caller is forced to conflate the two.

findings.title: Don't swallow missing-key errors in load()
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent, and that error propagated to callers. The added catch-all now maps that failure (and any other error, e.g. a store.get that throws) to the empty string. loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps keys through load, so a missing key now yields "" in the returned array, exactly the same value a key present-but-empty would produce. Callers can no longer detect the failure and may treat/persist/report the empty fallback as real data. Because load is an exported public API, the unusable contract is itself the defect even though the only in-repo caller is loadAll.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures and cannot report failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly added retryBackground catches every error with a bare `catch { continue; }` (src/retry.ts:27-29) and returns void, so when fn() throws on every attempt the function returns normally and the caller cannot distinguish 'succeeded' from 'exhausted all retries without success'. The error is neither rethrown, logged, nor surfaced through a return value/callback. Because it is an exported public function with no in-repo callers yet, the unusable contract ships now: every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Renaming timeoutMs->timeout + required retries breaks Config callers
findings.whyItBreaks: `Config` is an exported interface. Removing `timeoutMs` and adding a required `retries` breaks every existing consumer that builds the old shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }`. TypeScript consumers get a compile error, but JS/`as any` consumers silently get `config.timeout === undefined`, so `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN and the `Date.now() > deadline` guard is never true (time budget stops working), and `config.retries === undefined` makes `i < undefined` false so `retryBackground` never runs `fn` at all.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows every error with no observable failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The added export catches every thrown error (`catch { continue; }`) and returns `void` when attempts are exhausted or the deadline trips. Neither the failure nor the last error is propagated or logged, so a caller cannot distinguish 'the operation succeeded' from 'every attempt failed'. For a fire-and-forget write/job this makes a total failure look identical to success, and callers may persist or report a fallback as if it were real.

findings.title: Rename of exported timeoutMs silently disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: `Config` is exported, but `timeoutMs` was removed and replaced with `timeout` with no compatibility shim. An existing consumer that still passes `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` (built dynamically) yields `config.timeout === undefined`, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined === NaN`. The guard `Date.now() > deadline` at src/retry.ts:10 (and :23) is then always false, so the wall-clock deadline is never enforced and `retry` can run all `maxAttempts` regardless of the intended timeout — a silent behavior regression rather than a compile error for dynamically-built configs.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows the terminal error and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: `catch { continue; }` discards every failure, and once the loop is exhausted the function returns void without rethrowing or logging the last error (src/retry.ts:20-30). As an exported/public API, every caller is forced to conflate "all attempts failed" with success; there is no signal at any decision point distinguishing the two, so a caller cannot retry-elsewhere, report, or compensate.

findings.title: value.length on string|number: TS error and len=undefined for numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` is now `string | number` (line 2), but line 6 reads `value.length`. TypeScript rejects this union access (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number', TS2339), so the file no longer type-checks. At runtime a numeric value has no `length`, so the label becomes the literal `len=undefined` instead of a length, and `defaultValue={label}` (line 7) renders that garbage.

findings.title: Field now renders a length label instead of the provided value
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the component rendered `defaultValue={value}`; now line 7 renders `defaultValue={label}` where `label` is `len=<n>` (line 6). Every existing string caller that relied on `Field` displaying the value now sees `len=3` instead of `abc`, a user-facing regression on the exported component's core behavior.

findings.title: Field input no longer displays its value; shows `len=<n>` instead
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the component rendered `defaultValue={value}`, i.e. the input was pre-filled with the passed value. The change computes `label = `len=${value.length}`` and renders `defaultValue={label}`, so every consumer now gets an input pre-filled with the literal string `len=5` (or `len=0` for an empty string) instead of the actual value. This is a user-facing regression for the component's only purpose and also drops the original value entirely.

findings.title: Widened `value` to `string | number` but body calls `value.length`
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` is now typed `string | number`, promising callers may pass a number. The body reads `value.length`, which does not exist on `number`: TypeScript reports TS2339 (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`), and at runtime a number yields `undefined`, so a numeric field renders the literal `len=undefined`. The type annotation's promise (numbers supported) is contradicted by the implementation and the value is silently corrupted.

findings.title: Widened value type but body assumes string (.length on number)
findings.whyItBreaks: The public interface now advertises `value: string | number` (src/components/Field.tsx:2), so numeric callers are legitimately allowed. The body computes `value.length` (src/components/Field.tsx:6), which is `undefined` for any number, so a numeric value renders `defaultValue="len=undefined"` instead of a real length. Under TypeScript this is also a compile error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'` on a `string | number` union), so the module does not type-check as written.

findings.title: Stop echoing secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` with TOKEN bound to `${{ secrets.TOKEN }}`, writing the repository secret into the Actions run log. GitHub log masking only redacts exact literal matches and is trivially defeated by any transformation (substring, encoding, surrounding text), and logs are retained and readable by anyone with repo/Actions read access — the credential can be recovered and reused. The same workflow triggers `on: push`, so this prints the secret on every push.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` with TOKEN set from `secrets.TOKEN` (line 11), so the deployment credential is written to the job's console log. GitHub's log masking is best-effort and only redacts the exact secret string; any truncation, transformation, or multi-line secret leaks the value, and Actions logs are readable by anyone with repository access. Exposing a deploy token this way can allow unauthorized deployments or lateral access.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 11 injects `secrets.TOKEN` into the step env and line 12 prints it via `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. Secrets echoed to stdout are persisted in the job log and are only concealed by GitHub's exact-string masking, which fails for secrets with leading/trailing whitespace, multi-line values, unset secrets, or once transformed (e.g. base64/JSON-encoded). Any reader of the workflow run (including forked-PR/lesser-privileged contexts) can obtain the deploy credential, which is a credential-exposure/security regression on a `push`-triggered deploy workflow.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; 1 MiB default breaks large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper previously passed maxBuffer: 64 MiB; it now relies on child_process.spawnSync's default of 1024*1024 (1 MiB). git() is used for the full PR patch via git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd) (line 140) and for git diff --name-only (line 57). When a diff exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/vendored files), spawnSync sets res.error (ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER), kills the child, and leaves res.status === null. The guard `res.status !== 0` (line 38) is therefore true and throws with empty stderr, so runGithub catches it and posts "Needlefish: review failed" / conclusion failure — a legit PR is blocked. Diff sizes that worked before now fail.

findings.title: Dropping git maxBuffer breaks review of large diffs (>1MB)
findings.whyItBreaks: This line removes maxBuffer: 64MB, so spawnSync falls back to Node's default maxBuffer of 1MB for both stdout and stderr. The same helper produces the full patch via git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd) at line 140 and the name-only list at line 57. For any PR whose git diff output exceeds 1MB, spawnSync kills the child, sets res.status to null and res.error to ENOBUFS, so `res.status !== 0` at line 38 is true and line 39 throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr. runGithub then falls into its catch block and posts 'Needlefish: review failed' for a PR that is perfectly reviewable — a regression versus the base revision, which allowed 64MB.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer: 1 MiB default fails on large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (1024*1024). All git() calls now run unbuffered against that cap, and git() is used at line 140 to capture the full `git diff mergeBase headSha` patch and at line 57 for `git diff --name-only`. Node's spawnSync returns status=null with an ENOBUFS error (stdout truncated) once the default 1 MiB is exceeded, so `res.status !== 0` is true and git() throws `git diff ... failed`. runGithub catch (line 182) then posts a `Needlefish: review failed` check and the review never runs. Previously the 64 MiB cap let large PRs (lockfiles, generated code, many-file diffs) succeed, so this is a regression for exactly the large PRs a review bot is most needed on.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The args array no longer includes `-s read-only`, so the spawned `codex exec` no longer pins its sandbox. With the flag removed, exec passes `sandbox_mode = None`, which resolves through config/trust defaults. In the installed codex-cli 0.160.1, when no `sandbox_mode`/`default_permissions` is configured and the project has a trust decision, the default permission profile is `:workspace` (workspace-write); codex-rs's own test `empty_config_defaults_to_builtin_profile_for_trusted_project` asserts `policy.can_write_local_path_with_cwd(cwd) == true` for exactly this shape (empty config + trusted project). This environment's `~/.codex/config.toml` contains `[projects."/tmp/needlefish-managed-MDXywb/runner-repo"] trust_level = "trusted"`, and `runCodex` spawns with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so the trusted key matches. Result: the automated review subprocess can now create/modify/delete files in the working tree under review instead of being denied writes, breaking the reviewer's non-mutating guarantee and making repo-supplied prompt injection able to mutate the checkout. Previously `-s read-only` forced read-only independent of trust/config.

findings.title: Re-pin read-only sandbox for the spawned codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops the explicit `-s read-only` flag from the `codex exec` argv. With no CLI sandbox, `codex exec` leaves sandbox_mode=None (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs, `sandbox_mode_cli_arg.map(...)`) and forces `approval_policy = Never` in headless mode, then resolves the effective sandbox from config. In the released 0.160.1 logic, `ConfigToml::derive_permission_profile` defaults a project that has a trust decision to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs:832-833), and workspace-write maps to a writable permission profile. This environment's `$HOME/.codex/config.toml` contains `[projects."/tmp/needlefish-managed-A9kW5r/runner-repo"] trust_level = "trusted"`, and runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=repoPath inheriting HOME/CODEX_HOME — so the agent now runs with workspace-write + no approvals instead of the previously pinned read-only sandbox. Because the prompt/context includes untrusted diff content, an injected instruction can write files or run local commands in the repo under review, defeating the read-only guarantee this line existed to enforce. Without the flag the guarantee is only as strong as ambient config, which may also be `danger-full-access`.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox: removal grants write access to reviewed repo
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd = opts.repoPath. The base code forced `-s read-only`; this diff deletes it, so the sandbox falls back to the ambient/default policy. In the codex source, `sandbox_mode_cli_arg.map(...)` yields None when `-s` is absent (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:331) and the config default resolves to the builtin workspace profile with `can_write_local_path_with_cwd(cwd, cwd) == true` on non-Windows (codex-rs/core/src/config/config_tests.rs:3587). The local CODEX_HOME config sets only `trust_level = "trusted"` and no `sandbox_mode`, so the effective policy becomes workspace-write. The spawned model can now create, modify, or delete files in the repository it is supposed to only review, defeating the read-only guarantee and turning any prompt-injection in the untrusted PR/diff into persisted filesystem writes.

findings.title: Restore merge-base/headSha scoping for the reviewed patch
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the reviewed range was computed as mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and then diff(mergeBase, headSha), so the patch/changedFiles contained only the PR's own changes. Now it is diff(baseSha, "HEAD") and changedFileSet(baseSha). This is a no-op only in the no-env default path because baseSha defaults to merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) and headSha defaults to HEAD. But PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA exist precisely so the caller supplies them (typical Actions usage sets PR_BASE_SHA to github.event.pull_request.base.sha, the base-branch tip, which is not necessarily an ancestor of the PR head). In that case diff(baseSha, HEAD) includes base-branch commits (shown reversed) and changedFileSet(baseSha) marks unrelated files as changed, so the reviewer analyzes and comments on code outside the PR and can return a wrong verdict. Additionally the tip is now the literal "HEAD" rather than headSha (line 137), while postReview/postCheck still post against headSha (lines 178-179) and bundle.headSha is set to headSha (line 165) — on a pull_request merge-ref checkout HEAD is the merge commit, so the analyzed patch and the annotated commit disagree.

findings.title: Diff from merge-base, not base SHA, to isolate PR changes
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `git diff merge-base(baseSha,headSha) headSha` with a raw two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` (and feeding `changedFileSet` the same `baseSha`) only yields the PR's own changes when `baseSha` is an ancestor of the local HEAD. `baseSha` comes from `PR_BASE_SHA` (the base-branch tip, e.g. `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`). If the workflow checks out the PR head (`HEAD == headSha`) and the base branch advanced past the fork after the PR branched, `merge-base(baseSha, HEAD) != baseSha`, so the two-dot diff reports every base-only commit as a reversion/deletion in `patch`, and `classifyFiles` receives base-only paths in `changedFiles`. That mislabels surfaces and makes `changedPaths` (line 141) filter inline comments against files the PR never touched. The removed line existed precisely to prevent this; note the original bug it guarded (headSha possibly not fetched locally) is still fixable without leaking base changes: `git merge-base baseSha HEAD` only needs local refs.

findings.title: Restore merge-base PR diff; baseSha..HEAD can review the wrong patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines computed mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and built the patch/changed-file set from mergeBase..headSha, i.e. exactly the commits the PR introduces. The new code (139) uses a two-dot diff `git diff baseSha HEAD` and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) (which itself diffs baseSha..HEAD at line 57). Two concrete problems: (1) dropping the merge base means that whenever baseSha is ahead of the PR's branch point (base branch advanced after branching, or PR targets a release branch), the diff shows those base-only commits as reverse changes and classifyFiles() lists base-branch-only files as changed — the reviewer then reviews and can inline-comment on files the PR never touched. (2) it diffs against the literal `HEAD` rather than the already-computed `headSha` (line 137, from `PR_HEAD_SHA`); in the GitHub Actions pull_request checkout `HEAD` is typically the merge commit, so the patch/changedFiles no longer correspond to the commit the review is posted against (`commit_id: headSha` at line 85, `head_sha: headSha` at line 124), which can also misalign inline-comment line numbers from core/review's patch parsing.

findings.title: Restore replacer functions: string replacement interprets `$&`/`$'`/`` $` ``/`$$` in bundle text
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace(search, replacement)` treats a *string* replacement as a template that expands `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` token, `$'`→the entire tail of the prompt after the match, and `` $` ``→the entire head before the match. The base used replacer *functions* (`() => JSON.stringify(...)`, `() => bundle.patch`), which take only the returned value and perform no `$` expansion. The head passes the raw data as a replacement string, so any `$&`, `$$`, `$'`, or `` $` `` occurring in the serialized bundle, in the candidate findings JSON, or in `bundle.patch` (a raw unified diff of arbitrary source, the most likely carrier) gets substituted instead of inserted literally. Concrete example: `'X{{BUNDLE}}Y'.replace('{{BUNDLE}}', '$&')` yields `X{{BUNDLE}}Y` — the payload is dropped and the placeholder token is spliced back in; `$'` would duplicate the whole remainder of the review prompt. The LLM then receives a mangled review prompt, degrading or silently changing the review verdict, with no error surfaced.

findings.title: String replacer re-expands $ patterns, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing a plain string as String.prototype.replace's replacement makes the JS engine interpret `$` substitution patterns: `$$`->`$`, `$&`->the matched substring, `` $` ``->the entire text preceding the match, `$'`->the entire text following the match (a `$1` with no capture group stays literal). bundle.patch is raw git diff text and is inserted both directly at line 33 and inside the JSON.stringify(bundle,...) at line 25 (JSON.stringify escapes quotes/newlines but NOT `$`, `'`, or backticks). Any shell/Makefile/regex/sed-style diff containing `$$`, `$&`, `$'`, or `` $` `` therefore gets rewritten before it reaches the model: `$$` collapses to `$`, `$&` is replaced by the `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` token itself, and `` $` ``/`$'` splice the whole surrounding prompt pre/post filler into the body, inflating and mangling the prompt. The base revision used function-form replacers (`() => JSON.stringify(...)`), which insert the value literally with no `$` interpretation, so this is a regression introduced by this diff. Observed behavior: in Node, `'{{PATCH}}'.replace('{{PATCH}}','a$$b $&')` yields `a$b {{PATCH}}`, whereas the function form yields `a$$b $&` unchanged.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$`-pattern corruption of injected text
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only treats the replacement literally when it is a function. When the replacement is a string (as now on lines 25/32/33), the patterns `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$n`, `$<name>` are expanded. The replacements here are `JSON.stringify(bundle)`, `JSON.stringify(candidate)`, and the raw PR diff `bundle.patch`; any of those containing a `$` sequence (e.g. a diff line like `+ s = s.replace(/x/, "$&y")` or a `$'`/`` $` ``/`$1` in shell, regex, or template code) gets rewritten: `$&` becomes the literal `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` match, `$'` appends the remainder of the template, and `` $` `` prepends the preceding text. The Codex prompt then reaches the model with corrupted/misframed bundle and patch content, silently degrading or invalidating the review. The original `() => ...` form existed precisely to keep the replacement verbatim.

findings.title: Malformed findings silently defaulted to P1/bug instead of rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base commit normalizeFinding threw on malformed input ('invalid severity', 'missing file', 'invalid lineStart', ...) and normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) propagated that error, so a malformed review was rejected (and the strict=false path dropped bad findings via try/catch). The new normalizeFinding never throws for object input: an invalid/absent severity becomes 'P1', an invalid category becomes 'bug', a missing file becomes '', an invalid lineStart/lineEnd becomes 0/NaN, and a missing title becomes 'Untitled finding'. Because normalizeReview now always uses this path (the strict parameter was also removed and had defaulted to true), no caller can distinguish malformed model output from a real finding; a garbage entry is surfaced as a high-severity (P1) bug anchored to file='' line 0. An exported, public swallow site that maps failure to a default value is the defect itself, independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Keep rejecting malformed findings instead of defaulting to P1/empty file
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeFinding threw on every malformed finding (non-object, invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd), and normalizeReview's non-strict path dropped those findings entirely (base src/shared/schema.ts:96-122,155-165). The new body coerces each bad field to a plausible default: invalid/missing severity → "P1" (line 98), invalid category → "bug" (line 100-102), empty title → "Untitled finding" (99), missing file → "" (103), missing lineStart/lineEnd → 0 (104-105). Because the `strict` parameter was also removed, normalizeReview always maps findings through this coercion (line 131), so callers can no longer distinguish a malformed finding from a genuine one: garbage is emitted as a P1 finding with file="" and lineStart=0 — exactly the shape the review contract forbids (every finding must cite a concrete changed file and line range) — and callers that relied on strict throwing to retry/flag needs_human lose that signal. Removing the `!raw || typeof raw !== "object"` guard additionally turns a null finding element into an uncaught TypeError inside normalizeReview instead of the prior descriptive throw/drop.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base normalizeFinding threw for every malformed field (not-an-object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-finite or <=0 lineStart/lineEnd). The head body replaces all of those throws with substitutions: severity -> 'P1', title -> 'Untitled finding', category -> 'bug', file -> '', lineStart/lineEnd -> 0. normalizeReview still maps every element through it (src/shared/schema.ts:131), so a truncated or hallucinated finding is emitted as a legitimate P1 finding with an empty path and zero line numbers rather than surfacing the parse failure. Callers can no longer distinguish 'the model produced garbage' from 'here is a real finding', while normalizeReview's retained structural throws (src/shared/schema.ts:114-130) make it look like validation still happens. Removing the `strict` parameter also silently changes the default from throw-on-malformed-finding to accept-as-default and makes any positional second argument a no-op.

findings.title: Restore -R when resolving PR refs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (steps lines 26-40) runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so the working directory is not a git repo with an `origin` remote on a fresh/cleaned/ephemeral self-hosted workspace. Without `-R "$REPO"` (env removed at line 29) and with no `GH_REPO` set, `gh pr view` cannot determine the repository: the gh 2.98 binary contains the error paths "failed to determine base repo: %w" / "no git remotes found" and contains no `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` reference at all (it only honors `--repo`/`-R`, `GH_REPO`, or the cwd git remote). Because the step uses `echo "head=$(gh ...)"`, bash's `-e` (GitHub's `bash -eo pipefail`) does NOT abort on the failed substitution — verified: `bash -eo pipefail -c 'echo "head=$(false)"'` exits 0 and prints `head=`. So the step succeeds while writing `head=` and `base=` (empty). Downstream this feeds `actions/checkout` `ref: ${{ steps.refs.outputs.head }}` (line 45), which with an empty ref checks out the default/triggering ref instead of the PR head, and passes empty `PR_HEAD_SHA`/`PR_BASE_SHA` to `src/cli.ts` (lines 56-57) — the run reviews the wrong commit or fails, silently. Previously `-R "$REPO"` made ref resolution independent of checkout state and it worked.

findings.title: Restore repo context for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (lines 26-40) runs before `Checkout PR head` (line 42), so at this point the workspace has no git checkout and no `origin` remote. Removing `-R "$REPO"` (and the `REPO` env) leaves `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` with no way to resolve the repository: gh only infers the repo from a local git remote, the `-R` flag, or `GH_REPO` -- not from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`. Verified locally with gh 2.98.0: in a non-git directory (even with GITHUB_ACTIONS=true and GITHUB_REPOSITORY set) it exits 1 with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`, whereas `-R frankekn/needlefish` / `GH_REPO=frankekn/needlefish` resolve fine. This branch (line 37-40 `else`) is taken on the documented `workflow_dispatch` manual trigger, where `github.event.pull_request` is null so `EVENT_HEAD` is empty; the normal `pull_request` path uses `EVENT_HEAD` and is unaffected.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch refs lookup breaks without -R (runs before checkout)
findings.whyItBreaks: The `else` branch executes only for `workflow_dispatch` (for `pull_request`, EVENT_HEAD at line 31 is always set, so lines 38-39 are skipped). This step runs before `actions/checkout` (line 43), so GITHUB_WORKSPACE is not a git checkout the workflow controls. `gh` resolves the target repo only from `-R`/`GH_REPO`/a git remote in the CWD; verified locally that without a checkout it aborts with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`. It does not fall back to `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified). Because the call is inside `echo "...$(gh ...)"`, the step does not fail: it writes `head=`/`base=` empty, `actions/checkout` then defaults to the triggering ref (default branch), and the review runs against the wrong code instead of the requested PR. On a clean/fresh self-hosted workspace (or when the manual trigger is the first run), `gh pr view` cannot resolve the repo at all.

findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) validates every finding in strict mode and throws on the first malformed one; with the added `false` the candidate pass takes the non-strict branch (map -> try/catch -> return null -> filter nulls), so a real P0/P1/P2 finding that is missing/invalid in exactly one required field (severity, category, file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix, lineStart/lineEnd) is deleted with no log and no error. candidate is the ONLY input to the critic ({{FINDINGS}}) and the critic only prunes, so the dropped finding cannot be recovered; the only gate, `!candidate.summary || candidate.checked.length === 0` (line 30), still passes, and findings come solely from pruned (line 43), so deriveVerdict returns `pass` where the base code (strict default) aborted loudly with a malformed-output error. Failure is no longer distinguishable from a legitimately empty findings list. Base line used the strict default; this call is now the lone lenient decode while the critic decode on line 38 stays strict.

findings.title: normalizeReview hides malformed review output as an empty valid review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw for a non-object payload, a missing/non-string summary, or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. The new body replaces every one of those throws with a default: `String(raw?.summary ?? "")`, `[]` for findings, `[]` for checked, `[]` for residual_risks. A malformed model response (e.g. `null`, a string, or an object missing `findings`) is therefore no longer distinguishable from a legitimate review that genuinely has no findings and no blocking risks — callers that persist/act on the normalized result will treat garbage as a clean 'pass, no findings, nothing blocks'. The removed guard at src/shared/schema.ts:125 (`summary`) also meant an empty summary now flows through as `""` rather than an error.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeReview threw on a non-object, a non-string/absent summary, and absent/non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks (base lines 115-131). Now every such failure is mapped to a default: summary becomes "", findings/checked/residual_risks become []. The resulting value is structurally identical to a legitimately valid review that found no issues, so any caller of this exported function can no longer tell 'the model returned unusable output' from 'review passed cleanly with no findings'. For a review gate this is a silent false-pass: malformed model output (null, a string, or an object missing findings) is accepted instead of surfacing the failure.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently downgrades malformed review output to a clean default
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, normalizeReview threw on malformed input: `!raw || typeof raw !== "object"`, `typeof raw.summary !== "string"`, `!Array.isArray(raw.findings)`, `!Array.isArray(raw.checked)`, and `!Array.isArray(raw.residual_risks)` all raised "malformed review output: ..." errors. The new body catches none of that — it maps a missing/non-array `findings`/`checked`/`residual_risks` to `[]` and a missing summary to `""` (lines 115-128). So `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview({})`, or `normalizeReview("<model garbage>")` now return `{ summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] }` instead of raising. Any caller that maps an empty RawReview to a passing verdict (no findings, no blocking residual risks) can no longer distinguish "the model produced an unusable/failed response" from "the model reviewed the diff and found nothing" — a malformed run is reported as a clean PASS. The function is exported (public contract), so every consumer is forced to conflate failure with a legitimate empty value.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path checks out wrong ref and sends empty SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still runs on workflow_dispatch (line 24 `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || ...`) and the trigger still requires a `pr_number` input (lines 10-14), but the old `Resolve PR refs` step that called `gh pr view` for manual runs was deleted. On a workflow_dispatch event `github.event.pull_request` is empty, so line 29 `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` falls back to `github.ref` (the branch the workflow was dispatched on, typically the default branch) instead of the PR head; line 35 defaults BASE_REF to 'main' regardless of the real PR base; and lines 45-46 interpolate to empty strings so PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are blank while line 47 still passes the real --pr number. The review tool therefore runs against the wrong checkout/base with no diff SHAs, silently reviewing the wrong revision (or failing). The pull_request path is unchanged and still correct.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch review checks out wrong ref; passes empty base/head SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still declares/supports `workflow_dispatch` (line 24 `if:` allows it, lines 10-14 require `pr_number`, line 47 still consumes `github.event.inputs.pr_number`), but the removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only place that resolved head/base for that trigger via `gh pr view`. On `workflow_dispatch` the `github.event.pull_request` payload is absent, so every expression reading it evaluates to empty: checkout `ref` (line 29) falls back to `github.ref` (whatever branch was selected in the dispatch UI, e.g. `main`) instead of the requested PR's head commit, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) become empty strings. The manual review therefore runs the tool against the wrong tree and with no base/head SHAs — the previously working manual-bypass trigger now silently reviews the wrong code.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path now reviews wrong ref with empty base/head SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is null, so github.event.pull_request.base.sha and github.event.pull_request.head.sha evaluate to empty strings. The old 'Resolve PR refs' step handled this branch by calling `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid,baseRefOid` and feeding those SHAs to PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA; that fallback is gone. The same null also breaks line 29 `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}`, which falls back to github.ref (the branch the workflow was dispatched on, i.e. the default branch) instead of the PR head, so the review checks out and reviews the wrong commit entirely. The `if:` at line 24 still admits workflow_dispatch, so this silent mis-review is reachable on the documented manual trigger (input description line 13 claims it reviews the given PR). Note: the `--pr` argument still receives the input number, but that does not repair the empty SHAs or the wrong checkout ref.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(); large diffs now abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: `spawnSync` defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024 (1 MiB). The git helper now runs without an explicit maxBuffer, and its main consumer is `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` (src/adapters/local.ts:100), whose full unified-diff output is the review payload. When that output exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, vendored deps, generated/dist files, large refactors), Node kills the child and sets `status` to null with `error.code = ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`. `res.status !== 0` (line 12) is then true, so it throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr — the entire `runLocal` flow fails before any review runs. Previously the 64 MiB cap covered these diffs. Note the sibling `gh` helper (line 33-36) still sets maxBuffer 64 MiB, so this is an asymmetric, unintended loss of the same protection.

findings.title: Restore large maxBuffer: git diff >1MB now fails the review
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 makes spawnSync fall back to Node's default maxBuffer of 1 MiB. The shared git() helper is used to capture the full patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) at src/adapters/local.ts:100. For any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB, Node terminates the child and sets res.status=null and res.error=ENOBUFS (verified in this runtime: status=null, error=ENOBUFS, stderr=""). Since res.status !== 0 is true, git() throws at line 13 with an empty stderr, so runLocal aborts and the tool can no longer review large PRs. Previously the 64 MiB buffer covered large diffs. Note the sibling gh() helper still keeps maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 (line 36), confirming git() losing it is an inconsistent regression, not an intentional tightening.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; 1 MiB default breaks large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The change drops `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the `git()` spawnSync call, reverting to Node's default of 1 MiB. `git()` is used at line 100 to capture the full `git diff <base> HEAD` patch, which routinely exceeds 1 MiB on real PRs (lockfiles, vendored/generated files). On overflow spawnSync terminates the child, sets `res.error = ENOBUFS`, leaves `res.status` null, and truncates stdout; the guard at line 12 (`res.status !== 0`) then throws `git diff ... failed: <empty stderr>`, so `runLocal` fails and no review is produced. Previously the same call worked up to 64 MiB. Note the sibling `gh()` at line 36 still keeps the 64 MiB cap, confirming the cap was intentional and its removal here is an unintended regression.

findings.title: Keep errored review check blocking, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block covers any failure from review()/postReview()/postCheck() and now posts the check-run conclusion as "neutral" (previously "failure"). GitHub treats neutral as a non-failing/mergeable conclusion for required status checks, so a PR whose review errored can satisfy branch protection without a completed review. The check title/summary still assert the review failed and "did NOT pass this PR", so the machine signal and the human text now disagree - the failure bit is downgraded to a default value that downstream gating cannot distinguish from a benign outcome (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Keep errored review check conclusion as failure, not neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now posts the `Needlefish` check-run with conclusion `neutral` instead of `failure`. `neutral` is the same non-blocking value the tool already emits for a legitimate `needs_human` verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION at src/adapters/github.ts:53), and branch-protection/merge gates that require the `Needlefish` check treat `neutral` as passing. So when `review()` (or postReview) throws — gh/git failure, unparseable diff, oversized input — the PR no longer fails the gate and can merge with no review, contradicting the check's own output text 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR'. This is a fail-open downgrade of the error signal versus the previous `failure` conclusion, which blocked.

findings.title: Errored review posts neutral check, unblocking merge
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block of runGithub the check-run conclusion was changed from "failure" to "neutral" (line 191) while the posted summary still claims `Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.` (line 193). Before this diff, a review that threw produced a failing 'Needlefish' check-run, which blocks merge under required-status-check branch protection. GitHub treats a `neutral` conclusion as non-blocking/passing for required checks (unlike `failure`), so after this change an errored review is reported as a pass to the gate, silently downgrading the failure signal the tool exists to enforce.
