findings.title: Lost severity normalization silently downgrades valid findings to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code computed `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before matching against SEVERITIES (exact uppercase list @src/shared/schema.ts:85). The head matches `raw.severity` directly and drops the coercion, so any severity that is not already exactly "P0".."P3" — lowercase/whitespace/cased model output like "p0", "P1 ", "p2", or a non-string — now fails `SEVERITIES.includes(...)` and is silently mapped to the default. Because the default was also changed from "P1" to "P3" (the lowest severity), a genuinely critical "p0" input is now recorded as "P3", i.e. a valid high-severity finding is misclassified and can be filtered/gated out downstream. `normalizeFinding` is exported, so this normalization contract (its whole purpose) is the public behavior every caller receives.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently downgrades mescased/whitespace severity to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation normalized the raw value first (`String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()`) before the SEVERITIES membership check, so inputs like `p1`, `p0`, or `P0 ` were correctly recognized. The changed body checks `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` directly against the exact uppercase literal, so any case/whitespace variant no longer matches and falls through to the fallback, which was also changed from `P1` to `P3`. Result: `raw.severity = "p0"` (a critical finding) is now emitted as `"P3"` instead of `"P0"`/`"P1"`, i.e. the highest-severity signal is silently classified as the lowest. This is a public exported normalizer whose returned severity is exactly what callers receive (only in-repo caller is normalizeReview @src/shared/schema.ts:132), so the misclassification propagates to every consumer of the review output.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and conservative fallback in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The function named normalizeFinding no longer normalizes: base code did `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and returned `sev` when it matched SEVERITIES, else "P1". The new body tests the raw value directly (`SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity) ? raw.severity : "P3"`). Two regressions follow: (1) previously-accepted inputs with case/whitespace variation ("p1", " p1 ", "P1\n") are no longer normalized and now fall through, and (2) the fallback for an absent/invalid severity changed from the escalated default "P1" to the lowest default "P3". Both silently downgrade a finding's severity — e.g. a critical finding emitted as "p0"/"P0 " now becomes P3 — which is a fail-open default on an exported review-output normalizer whose severity feeds verdict decisions. normalizeReview@src/shared/schema.ts:132 passes untrusted `any` JSON (LLM output) into this function, so non-canonical severity strings are a realistic input.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision built a sanitized env (`const env = { ...process.env }; delete env.GH_TOKEN; delete env.GITHUB_TOKEN; delete env.GITHUB_API_TOKEN;`) and passed it via `env,` to spawnSync. This diff deletes both the sanitized env object and the `env,` option, so the child process now inherits the parent's full environment. As a result the codex CLI (and any process it spawns, since it runs with `-s read-only` but full env inheritance) receives live GitHub credentials, where previously they were withheld. This is a concrete secret-exposure regression introduced by these changed lines, not a style concern.

findings.title: Stop leaking GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN to the codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: This change removes `const env = { ...process.env }` plus the three `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` lines and no longer passes `env` to spawnSync. Node's child_process.spawnSync defaults `env` to process.env when omitted, so the codex child now receives every parent environment variable verbatim, including the GitHub credentials that were previously stripped. The child runs `codex exec` over untrusted review input (the PR diff/prompt) while holding these tokens, so injected content can read and exfiltrate them; `-s read-only` restricts filesystem writes only and does not filter the environment.

findings.title: Repo child process now inherits GitHub tokens after env scrub removed
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, a copy of process.env had GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted and was passed as `env` to spawnSync, so the `codex exec` child (which runs a model-driven, read-only shell session) never received GitHub credentials. The diff removes both the `delete env.*` lines and the `env,` field of the spawnSync options, so the child now falls back to the default behavior of inheriting the full parent environment — reintroducing the tokens into a subprocess whose output/content the model controls. This is a deliberate secret-leak defense being deleted, not an incidental refactor.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control restricting this job to PRs originating from the base repository. With it gone, a `pull_request` event from any fork now schedules the `review` job on `runs-on: self-hosted`. The job checks out the fork's PR head SHA (line 23) and then executes repo-controlled code with the fork's content: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, which runs dependency/workspace lifecycle scripts such as `prepare`/`postinstall`) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34). A malicious fork PR can therefore achieve arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted runner (persistent, typically networked and reused across jobs) without any approval, and the env block also hands it `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (line 33). This is exactly the threat the removed predicate was defending against.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: untrusted fork PRs execute on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control restricting this job to same-repo (internal) PRs. With it gone, the `on: pull_request` trigger will schedule the `review` job for PRs from forks as well. The job then checks out the fork's head commit (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, line 23) and executes it on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs any lifecycle/install scripts the fork controls, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr ...` (line 34) runs the fork's own source. That is arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host by any fork author (or, for a public repo, any GitHub user), enabling runner poisoning, exfiltration of the machine's credentials/state, and compromise of subsequent jobs. A self-hosted runner must never execute untrusted fork PR code.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` allows the `review` job to run for PRs from forks. This job uses `runs-on: self-hosted` and (a) checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (untrusted fork-controlled ref), (b) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (lifecycle/install scripts from untrusted package.json + lockfile), and (c) executes `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR's own `src/`. A contributor only needs to open a fork PR to obtain arbitrary code execution on the persistent self-hosted runner, where it can access runner-local credentials, caches, and network-reachable internal resources, and can tamper with subsequent CI. The removed predicate was the sole control restricting this job to same-repo (trusted) PRs.

findings.title: Silently overrides explicit 0 for runner kill grace/give-up
findings.whyItBreaks: With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, the old predicate `parsed >= 0` returned 0, so setTimeout(...) at line 124 fired on the next tick (immediate SIGKILL after SIGTERM). The new predicate `parsed > 0` rejects 0 and returns the fallback 5000 (line 5), so the kill sequence now waits 5s before SIGKILL. Same for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0: line 123 now waits 2000ms (fallback line 9) before finishing instead of giving up immediately. The operator's explicit 0 duration is silently discarded in favor of a built-in default, so a config intended to hard-kill/abort immediately now can add up to ~7s of extra latency on the failure path.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration from env now silently replaced by fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation accepted `parsed >= 0`, i.e. it deliberately treated a parsed `0` as valid. The new `parsed > 0` rejects `0` and returns `fallbackMs` instead. This function is the sole reader of `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS` (src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-6) and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS` (src/shared/runner-process.ts:7-10). Those constants feed the kill-sequence timers: `RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS` at line 123 (wait after SIGKILL before giving up on child close) and `RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS` at line 124 (SIGTERM→SIGKILL grace). Setting either env var to `0` was a legitimate way to disable that wait (0 = immediate); after this change it is silently overridden with 5000/2000ms, so a user who configured `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` now blocks up to 2s per kill and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` no longer kills immediately. No guard downstream justifies rejecting 0 — `setTimeout` accepts 0 natively.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so every changed file is deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge still truncates hotspots with slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 @src/core/review.ts:26), but the tail-coverage backstop that appended a hotspot for every changed file not covered by the selected hotspots was removed. Any changed file in a dropped hotspot (ranked below the top 6) or omitted by the map pass is now silently excluded from deep review. No residual risk or checked entry records the omission, so the returned verdict can be a pass over files that were never inspected.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded to [] and res.residual_risks from each deep pass (line 103) is never read; the old residuals array that collected them into candidateMerged is gone. The final residual risks come only from pruned.residual_risks (line 128) whose critic input had an empty residual_risks list, so a blocking residual (blocks:true) found during deep review can never reach deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) — a verdict that was previously blocked can now conclude pass.

findings.title: Forward deep-review residual risks to the critic again
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded to []. In the base, per-hotspot res.residual_risks (and blocks:true failure residuals) were accumulated into `residuals` and forwarded to the critic. The final result returns `pruned.residual_risks` (line 128), so blocking residual risks flagged during deep review are no longer fed into the critic and can vanish from the verdict gate (`deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` line 122) unless the critic independently re-derives them. This discards a risk signal the pipeline previously carried.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so no changed file is silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: After `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (max 6) the tail-coverage hotspot was removed. Any changed file that the map pass did not place in a selected hotspot — or that fell outside the top 6 — is no longer deep-reviewed. The base explicitly guaranteed every changed file got deep-reviewed ('never silently skip a changed file'); without it such files pass unreviewed.

findings.title: Do not let one hotspot failure abort the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed. Base caught a throwing runCodex/normalizeReview/extractJson (e.g. malformed LLM JSON), recorded a blocks:true residual, and continued to review the remaining hotspots. Now any single hotspot failure propagates out of reviewLarge, so one bad response returns no ReviewResult at all for the whole large PR.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop: changed files can now be skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deleted the tail-coverage block that pushed every changed file not covered by a selected hotspot into an extra hotspot. Now the loop at line 97 iterates only over `sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93, cap 6). Any changed file the map pass failed to assign to a hotspot, or assigned to a hotspot that falls outside the top 6, is never passed to deep.md/runCodex, so its findings are never produced — and reviewLarge can still return a PASS verdict. The tool silently certifies as reviewed a PR whose changed file(s) were never examined.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks are dropped before the critic/verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, previously accumulated into `residuals` and forwarded via `candidateMerged.residual_risks` so the critic could carry unresolved/blocking concerns into deriveVerdict. This PR hardcodes `residual_risks: []`, and the removal of the collector means every residual risk a deep pass reports (e.g. 'could not verify X') is discarded before the critic. The critic only receives patchStat for large PRs, so it cannot re-derive them; the final verdict can therefore pass while deep passes flagged blocking unknowns.

findings.title: One deep-pass failure now aborts the entire large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch that previously caught a failed deep pass (recording a `blocks: true` residual and continuing) was removed. `runCodex`/`extractJson`/`normalizeReview` for any one of up to 6 hotspots now throw out of the loop and out of reviewLarge, so a single transient model/parse failure makes the whole large review reject instead of returning findings from the other hotspots with a blocking residual risk. This is a graceful-degradation regression introduced by this PR.

findings.title: Deep pass no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}}; --focus silently dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: The head removes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep-prompt build (and also removes `focus: bundle.focus` from mapBundle at lines 86-88). deep.md's contract still ends with `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)`, so the rendered deep prompt now ships the literal token `{{FOCUS}}` instead of the user's lens, and map.md's documented rule ('If a `focus` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher') can never match because focus is no longer in the map bundle. The `--focus` option and Bundle.focus remain live (small-review path still forwards the whole bundle), so focus still works for small PRs but is silently ignored for large PRs — exactly where the large path runs. This is a contract drift: the deep.md carrier promises focus prioritization, the body no longer supplies it.

findings.title: Large reviews silently drop user-supplied focus directive
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep-prompt chain (was old line 120) and deletes `focus: bundle.focus` / `deep: bundle.deep` from `mapBundle` (was old lines 89-90), while the `Bundle.focus` field and its CLI/API surface are untouched and `reviewSmall` still forwards the whole bundle (src/core/review.ts:52-55). So for large PRs a user's `focus` is never delivered to the mapper or the per-hotspot deep pass. The base code's explicit `{{FOCUS}}` substitution plus the `?? "(none)"` default are direct evidence `deep.md` declares a `{{FOCUS}}` slot; with the replace removed, that placeholder is left as the literal token in the prompt and the requested focus is silently ignored, producing a different (unfocused) review than the user asked for and inconsistent large-vs-small behavior.

findings.title: Large-PR deep pass silently drops caller focus
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep-prompt construction (base f5568bd:122) and also removes `focus`/`deep` from `mapBundle` (base f5568bd:89-90). After the change, `bundle.focus` is referenced nowhere in `reviewLarge`: `rg -n focus src/core/review.ts` returns no hits in the head file. So for any PR that takes the large path (patch > 30000 chars or >10 changed files, src/core/review.ts:26-28), the user-supplied `focus` no longer reaches any prompt, while `reviewSmall` still forwards the entire bundle (including `focus`) via `JSON.stringify(bundle)` at src/core/review.ts:52-55. The result is inconsistent, silent behavior: the same `focus` input steers a small-PR review but is dropped for a large-PR review, and if `prompts/deep.md` still contains the `{{FOCUS}}` token (only review.ts is in this diff, so deep.md is unchanged) the model now receives the literal string `{{FOCUS}}`.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit invalid "Nm 60s" after independent rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) is not carried into minutes, so it can equal 60. For ms=119999: minutes=Math.floor(119999/60000)=1 and seconds=Math.round(59999/1000)=60, producing "1m 60s" (base code produced "2m 0s"). For minutes=0 (ms=59500) it prints "60s" instead of "1m 0s". Any duration whose remainder falls in [59500,60000) formats incorrectly.

findings.title: formatDuration emits "1m 60s" since seconds rounds without carrying
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes with Math.floor(ms/60000) and seconds with Math.round((ms % 60000)/1000) independently, so the rounded remainder can equal 60. For ms=119999: minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59.999)=60 → renders "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s"; for ms=59999 → "60s" instead of "1m 0s". The previous implementation rounded to total seconds first (totalSeconds = Math.round(ms/1000)) so totalSeconds % 60 could never be 60, meaning this diff introduces the malformed output. formatDuration is called for every stats entry and the total on the rendered review markdown (src/shared/render.ts:75, src/shared/render.ts:80), so the wrong duration is user-visible.

findings.title: formatDuration can render seconds as 60
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms while seconds is rounded from the remainder, so the two are computed independently and the remainder can round up to 60. For any ms in [59500, 59999] the result is '60s' (old code produced '1m 0s'), and for [119500, 119999] the result is '1m 60s' (old code produced '2m 0s'). A 60-second field is invalid display output and contradicts the old rounding-then-decompose behavior. This is rendered into user-facing PR review markdown via renderMarkdown at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its positive-only contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's name and its unchanged error text ('requires a positive integer') promise rejection of every non-positive integer, but changing the guard from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes 0 pass: Number.isInteger(0) is true and 0 < 0 is false, so the throw is skipped and 0 is returned as if valid. The body no longer implements the promised validation, and the error thrown for -1 now contradicts the silently accepted 0. Any consumer relying on this public validator to guarantee a strictly positive value (count, retry, port, timeout-style numeric input) receives 0 instead of an error.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now returns 0, breaking its positive contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported predicate changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 now passes. `Number("0")`, `Number("-0")`, `Number("")`, and `Number(" ")` all produce 0 and are now accepted and returned, while the function name `parsePositiveInteger` and the thrown message `"${label} requires a positive integer"` promise strict positivity (0 is not a positive integer). Because this is an exported public API with no in-repo callers, the promise itself is the contract: any consumer using the result as a guaranteed-positive value (e.g. `timeoutMs`, retry counts, batch/page sizes, divisors) now receives 0, causing disabled timeouts, zero-length allocations, or division-by-zero, and can no longer distinguish an invalid input from a legitimate 0.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its positive contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes 0 pass the guard, so the function returns a non-positive value while its exported name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its unchanged error text ('${label} requires a positive integer') both promise a strictly positive integer. Because `Number("")` and `Number("  ")` both evaluate to 0, empty/whitespace/unset input now silently returns 0 instead of throwing, so any caller cannot distinguish a legitimate value from missing/invalid input, and using the result as a count/size/loop bound would operate on 0.
